title: Ang 723–727: Tilang's close
hook: Guru Tegh Bahadur, Kabir and Namdev
tomorrow: why does shiny bronze leave black on your fingers?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tilang began: as the Word comes, Lalo, so I speak it. Truth to power. Today Tilang ends, and it takes three voices to close it.
screen: `TRUTH TO POWER.` → `THREE VOICES TO CLOSE IT.`

segments.voice: Your water bottle has a hairline crack nobody noticed, and now the bottom of your bag is soaked. Not all at once. Drip by drip. In Tilang, Guru Tegh Bahadur reaches for the same picture. In paraphrase: if you're going to wake up, wake up now, night and day; moment by moment your life slips away, like water from a cracked clay pot. The crack is there. The water is going. So is it already too late?
screen: `A HAIRLINE CRACK.` → `LIKE WATER FROM A CRACKED POT.` → `IS IT ALREADY TOO LATE?`

segments.voice: His answer comes at the end of the same hymn. In paraphrase: why don't you sing God's praises, caught in false greed, forgetting death? Even now, nothing is lost, if you sing God's praise. Nanak says, that's how you reach the state without fear. Listen to what that does to the pot. The crack is real, the water is leaving, and the Guru doesn't pretend otherwise. But he won't call it too late either. Then Tilang closes with two more voices. Kabir, a weaver in tradition, on ang 727, tells his brother: be still, even for a moment, and God is right there, present. And Namdev: I'm blind, and your Name, Creator, is my walking stick; I'm poor and meek, and your Name is my support. So the last pages of Tilang hold a Guru, a weaver, and a calico printer in tradition, from different trades and times, set side by side on one page. Three lives, one closing chord: wake up now, it isn't too late, and the Name is there to lean on. Three voices.
screen: `EVEN NOW, NOTHING IS LOST.` · `KABIR: BE STILL A MOMENT.` · `NAMDEV: YOUR NAME, MY STICK.` · `A GURU, A WEAVER, A PRINTER.` · then, large: `THREE VOICES.`

segments.voice: Pour a little water and take one slow sip. Hold it in your mouth a moment before you swallow, cool, and already on its way. Then sit with the breath, which comes and goes the same way, and isn't gone yet.
Ang 723. Where Tilang's last pages begin, closing with three voices: Guru Tegh Bahadur, Kabir and Namdev.
Three voices, one ending: even now, nothing is lost, and the Name is there to lean on. Fifteen thirty-four, and onward.

howItsDone: Guru Tegh Bahadur's Tilang hymns, Kabir's and Namdev's among them at the raga's close, are sung in kirtan; Namdev's 'your Name is the walking stick of the blind' is often quoted by Sikhs.

fork.setup: your grandfather says he's too old now to learn the instrument he always wanted to play. what fits Tilang's close?
options: agree gently; some cracks mean the chance is gone.
tell him to wait until life is calmer and there's more time.
even now, nothing is lost: start with what's in the pot.
fork.reveal: Guru Tegh Bahadur names the crack honestly, then says even now nothing is lost. wake up now, not later.

original.note: Gurmukhi: ghat, a clay pot, also the body; phootai ghat jio paanee, like water from a cracked pot (Tilang, Mahala 9).

trapdoor: what you thought: a cracked pot means it's too late.
what it means: Guru Tegh Bahadur says life slips away like water from a cracked pot, and that even now nothing is lost.
what a scholar hears: chhin chhin audh bihaat hai phootai ghat jio paanee; ajahoo kachh bigario nahee, Tilang, Mahala 9.
guess: where Suhi, the raga of union, opens
recall: as the word comes: truth to power

chat.says: 3 people giving speeches at navi's reception and they all say totally different stuff. is that a mess?
options: Not a mess. Tilang closes on three voices: different lives, one ending.
Yes. They should agree on one script so it sounds like one voice.
Only if one is the main speech and the other two just echo it.
chat.meaning: Tilang closes with Guru Tegh Bahadur, Kabir and Namdev: different trades and times, set on one page, landing on one ending.
